newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. seen taking difficult stand on Cambodian PM.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen taking difficult stand on Cambodian PM.

text.p: Washington's refusal to recognise a replacement for Cambodia's ousted first prime minister is a clear signal to other nations that it will not readily accept the overthrow of an elected leader, analysts said on Thursday.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted his co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a bloody coup on July 6.
"The U.S. is sending a very powerful message that the prince cannot just be removed by one man, by Hun Sen," a local political analyst said.
"Any removal must go back to the people. The prince was legitimately put in place by the 1993 election."
On Wednesday, the remnants of Ranariddh's royalist party nominated Foreign Minister Ung Huot, a senior member of the FUNCINPEC party, to succeed him.
But in a move that surprised many in Phnom Penh, the United States refused to recognise Ung Huot as the new co-prime minister, saying his selection was undemocratic.
"The U.S. is sending a message to other countries which are on the verge of recognising this government, like France, Japan and even southeast Asian countries," one analyst said.
"The U.S. can't accept a coup d'etat as a fait accompli," he said.
Hun Sen has moved swiftly to try to legitimise his hold on Cambodia since the coup.
Some diplomatic sources have reported widespread human rights abuses, including the killing of up to 40 of the prince's supporters.

Hun Sen has portrayed his ouster of Ranariddh as a move against Khmer Rogue guerrillas, who he says Ranariddh was using to bolster his military strength, and has said he was still committed to his coalition with FUNCINPEC and free and fair elections next year.
The replacement of Ranariddh as first prime minister was one more step in Hun Sen's legitimisation effort, analysts said.
Washington's rejection of Ung Huot has derailed, or at least delayed, Hun Sen's plans to gradually regain support from the international community, the analysts said.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns urged the authorities in Phnom Penh not to announce a new prime minister until FUNCINPEC "has an opportunity to make a reasoned decision on this matter, free of coercion, free of intimidation."
However, analysts said the U.S. position may prove untenable.
"What I suspect they (the U.S.) are up to is simply registering their continued disapproval of the situation, of what has happened over the last 10 days," said one Phnom Penh-based diplomat.

"But it's a difficult position to maintain simply because it doesn't seem realistic for Ranariddh to return and resume his duties. If that if the case, then another first prime minister has to be appointed," the diplomat said.
Ranariddh left Cambodia two days before his overthrow and has since called for resistance to Hun Sen and lobbied for support in Europe and the United States.
Thailand's foreign minister said on Thursday that Ranariddh was in Rome and would fly to Bangkok for a Friday meeting with several southeast Asian foreign ministers.
Hun Sen has said the prince was free to return to Cambodia but would face trial for his illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrillas and for alleged weapons smuggling.
"I don't believe it's possible to return to the previous situation with Prince Ranariddh as first prime minister," said a foreign Cambodia scholar. "I don't see a possibility for compromise."

Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party won a U.N.-organised election in 1993 but agreed to a coalition with Hun Sen, leader of Cambodia's former government, after Hun Sen objected to the poll result and the country faced division along factional lines.
While the chances of Ranariddh making a come-back were slim for now, Washington was obliged to make a stand, the first analyst said.
"A reversal of the situation will be very difficult on the ground in Cambodia but that's the position the U.S. must take if it wants to be the leader of the democratic world."
